title: Clinical Shift foundations and rotation practice
reviewStatus: Local source and consistency checks recorded September 7, 2026. Independent clinician review remains pending for all 18 encounters.

rotations.name: Emergency Medicine
rotations.description: Prioritize urgent problems, interpret new data, and decide what happens next.

rotations.name: Cardiology
rotations.description: Connect symptoms, examination findings, testing, and treatment decisions.

rotations.name: Neurology
rotations.description: Localize the problem, rank a differential, and protect the patient from dangerous misses.

em-016.assessment: 32-year-old hemodynamically stable woman with abrupt recurrent regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 188 bpm without visible P waves, terminated by adenosine, consistent with AVNRT. Post-conversion ECG, electrolytes, and TSH are normal, with no pre-excitation or ischemic changes.
em-016.plan: Acute episode managed per the stable-SVT pathway: modified Valsalva failed, and rapid IV adenosine (6 mg, then 12 mg) converted her to sinus rhythm on continuous monitoring. After observation, discharge with return precautions, caffeine reduction, instruction in vagal maneuvers, and outpatient cardiology follow-up; discuss elective ablation if episodes become frequent or poorly tolerated.

em-018.assessment: 50-year-old man on warfarin with delayed headache, confusion, gait instability, and focal right-sided findings after head trauma. CT shows a 12-mm left crescentic mixed-density extra-axial collection crossing sutures with 6-mm midline shift, consistent with an acute-on-subacute subdural hematoma with mass effect; INR 3.8.
em-018.plan: Hold warfarin and urgently reverse anticoagulation with four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K, rechecking INR after infusion to confirm correction. Obtain immediate neurosurgical consultation for operative evacuation, admit to an ICU for close neurologic and intracranial-pressure monitoring with repeat imaging, and avoid restarting anticoagulation until neurosurgery determines it is safe.

em-015.assessment: 78-year-old man with recurrent abrupt syncope and symptomatic bradycardia. ECG shows complete AV dissociation with atrial rate 88, ventricular escape 38, and wide QRS, confirming third-degree AV block.
em-015.plan: Stop AV-nodal-blocking medication, place the patient on continuous monitoring with pacing pads, and begin transcutaneous pacing with analgesia/sedation, confirming both electrical and mechanical capture, while preparing for urgent transvenous pacing (epinephrine or dopamine infusion as backup if capture fails). Obtain cardiology or electrophysiology consultation and arrange permanent pacemaker implantation; evaluate reversible contributors (trend the pending troponin to exclude acute ischemia; check potassium and magnesium) and admit to a monitored CCU bed, but do not delay pacing in this symptomatic patient.

em-020.assessment: 59-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes and septic physiology, rapidly progressive perineal pain out of proportion, necrosis, crepitus, and CT-demonstrated soft-tissue gas. Findings are consistent with Fournier gangrene and sepsis with hypoperfusion (hypotension, lactate 4.2 mmol/L) and acute kidney injury.
em-020.plan: Activate surgery immediately for debridement while starting broad IV antibiotics, cultures, and resuscitation. Use balanced crystalloid with frequent assessment of perfusion and fluid tolerance; add norepinephrine when hypotension persists or shock severity warrants concurrent support. One empiric option is vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam, with toxin-suppressing therapy when indicated. Adjust to renal function and microbiology. ICU care, repeat operative assessment, glucose management, and wound reconstruction follow source control.

em-033.assessment: 29-year-old woman at approximately 7 weeks' gestation with acute abdominal pain, shock, hemoglobin 8.1, positive hCG, empty uterus, left adnexal mass, and intraperitoneal free fluid, consistent with ruptured ectopic pregnancy and hemorrhagic shock. Blood type O negative.
em-033.plan: Stabilize airway, breathing, and circulation; place large-bore IV access, type and cross, and activate blood-product resuscitation with O-negative packed red cells as needed. Obtain immediate obstetric and gynecologic surgical intervention by laparoscopy or laparotomy, admit postoperatively to a monitored bed for ongoing hemodynamic and transfusion surveillance, trend CBC, coagulation, and hemodynamics, and administer Rho(D) immune globulin.

cd-001.assessment: 61-year-old man with reproducible exertional substernal pressure relieved by rest, unchanged over three months. Exercise ECG reproduced symptoms with 1.5-mm horizontal ST depression in V4-V6, supporting chronic stable angina with suspected obstructive coronary disease; coronary anatomy has not yet been demonstrated; no resting or unstable features are present.
cd-001.plan: Begin a beta-blocker such as metoprolol succinate for symptom control and prescribe sublingual nitroglycerin with use and emergency instructions. Start aspirin 81 mg daily and high-intensity atorvastatin with adherence counseling, plus smoking cessation, blood-pressure control, and close cardiology follow-up; escalate anatomic evaluation if symptoms persist or risk increases.

cd-006.assessment: 68-year-old man with new symptomatic atrial fibrillation and rapid ventricular response at 138-152 bpm, hemodynamically stable, likely precipitated by an alcohol binge. Troponin, electrolytes, TSH, and chest radiograph show no alternate acute trigger; CHA2DS2-VASc score is 3.
cd-006.plan: Use IV diltiazem for acute rate control with telemetry. Start long-term anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban after bleeding-risk review, counsel alcohol reduction, obtain echocardiographic and cardiology follow-up, and reassess rhythm-control options based on duration, symptoms, and anticoagulation status.

cd-055.assessment: 17-year-old athlete with exertional syncope, exertional chest tightness, family history of sudden death, and a systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva. ECG and echocardiography show asymmetric septal hypertrophy, systolic anterior motion, mitral regurgitation, and a resting LVOT gradient of 60 mmHg, confirming obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with high-risk syncope.
cd-055.plan: Pause intense competitive sports pending specialist evaluation and start a nonvasodilating beta-blocker. Refer urgently to a hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy and electrophysiology center for sudden-death risk stratification — including ambulatory ECG monitoring and cardiac MRI — and ICD evaluation, counsel hydration and avoidance of preload-reducing drugs, use shared decision-making about later exercise participation, and screen all first-degree relatives with ECG and echocardiography with genetic counseling as appropriate.

cd-061.assessment: 26-year-old man who injects drugs with 10 days of fever, a tricuspid regurgitation murmur, leukocytosis, and bilateral peripheral cavitary pulmonary nodules, highly concerning for Staphylococcus aureus tricuspid-valve infective endocarditis with septic pulmonary emboli.
cd-061.plan: Admit for respiratory support, prompt cultures, IV antibiotics, and complication assessment. Include MRSA coverage while choosing the full empiric regimen with infectious disease input; narrow to an antistaphylococcal beta-lactam for confirmed MSSA when tolerated. Obtain TTE promptly, using TEE when indicated. Repeat cultures to establish clearance and individualize antibiotic duration and surgical assessment to the organism, valve findings, response, and complications. Follow pending HIV and hepatitis testing, and offer addiction treatment and harm-reduction support.

cd-019.assessment: 39-year-old woman three weeks postpartum with inferior STEMI and angiographic RCA dissection. Initially preserved coronary flow allowed monitored conservative management, but later recurrent ischemia and hypotension indicate deterioration requiring urgent reassessment.
cd-019.plan: Activate urgent repeat coronary assessment and revascularization planning with interventional cardiology and cardiac surgery because ischemia and hypotension have recurred. Continue monitored supportive care and avoid thrombolysis for known SCAD. After stabilization, individualize antiplatelet and other treatment to the intervention and clinical course; arrange rehabilitation, extracoronary vascular assessment, and specialist counseling about recurrence, breastfeeding-compatible medications, and future pregnancy.

nr-011.assessment: 58-year-old woman with brief position-triggered vertigo and no auditory or focal neurologic symptoms. Right Dix-Hallpike testing produces delayed, transient, fatigable upbeating-torsional nystagmus, confirming right posterior-canal BPPV.
nr-011.plan: Repeat an appropriate Epley maneuver for the documented recurrence of right posterior-canal BPPV, after checking mobility and neck limitations. Avoid routine scheduled vestibular suppressants. Give fall advice and suitable home instructions, and reassess within one month; persistent, atypical, or central findings require further evaluation.

nr-025.assessment: 24-year-old man with a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure, postictal confusion, lateral tongue injury, and incontinence. Glucose, electrolytes, toxicology, CT, MRI, and EEG are normal, supporting a first unprovoked seizure without an identified structural lesion.
nr-025.plan: Discuss recurrence risk, benefits and adverse effects of medication, occupation, and the patient’s preferences with prompt neurology follow-up. Deferring medication is one reasonable option; normal tests do not eliminate recurrence risk. Give practical seizure precautions and applicable driving guidance, and clear return instructions for another or prolonged event.

nr-012.assessment: 45-year-old man with 18 hours of continuous acute vestibular syndrome. HINTS by a trained examiner favors a peripheral pattern, with an abnormal right head impulse, unidirectional left-beating nystagmus, and no skew; hearing is intact and no focal deficits are present, consistent with right vestibular neuritis.
nr-012.plan: Provide brief symptom relief and early vestibular rehabilitation. Discuss uncertain steroid benefit. Reassess promptly for new neurologic or auditory findings, severe gait impairment, or other atypical evolution; activate stroke assessment when concern persists.

nr-016.assessment: 22-year-old man after temporal head trauma with a lucid interval followed by rapid neurologic decline, left pupillary dilation, and right weakness. CT shows a 22-mm left biconvex epidural hematoma with temporal fracture, 9-mm midline shift, and early uncal herniation, consistent with middle meningeal artery injury.
nr-016.plan: Secure the airway and ventilation as needed and activate neurosurgery for immediate craniotomy and evacuation. While moving to the operating room, elevate the head 30 degrees with the neck midline, give hypertonic saline or mannitol, use only brief controlled hyperventilation for active herniation, prevent hypoxia and hypotension, maintain cervical spine precautions until cleared, and start 7-day post-traumatic seizure prophylaxis (levetiracetam).

nr-008.assessment: 38-year-old man with right neck and facial pain after cervical manipulation, painful partial Horner syndrome, and transient contralateral sensory symptoms. CTA shows flame-shaped right internal-carotid narrowing with intramural hematoma, confirming internal carotid artery dissection without established infarct.
nr-008.plan: Admit to a monitored stroke unit for serial neurologic checks, begin antithrombotic therapy with an antiplatelet agent or anticoagulation after contraindication review, obtain stroke and neurology consultation, and monitor for cerebral or retinal ischemia. Avoid further neck manipulation, arrange follow-up vascular imaging, and reserve endovascular treatment for recurrent ischemia or selected refractory disease.

em-101.assessment: A brief event during a characteristic trigger with prodrome, pallor and rapid recovery is most consistent with a vasovagal faint. Brief jerks are part of the witness account; they do not independently establish epilepsy. Current assessment identifies no cardiac red flag.
em-101.plan: Explain the working interpretation, document the patient and witness accounts plus ECG assessment, discuss trigger avoidance and what to do if symptoms recur, and arrange follow-up. Reassess a recurrent or changed event. Exertional collapse or a concerning family history would change urgency; neither belongs to this original presentation.

cd-101.assessment: A symptomatic fall from 148/82 lying to 112/64 after one minute standing supports postural hypotension. Recent medication and intake changes are possible contributors. Persistence after initial measures leaves the cause incompletely resolved.
cd-101.plan: Document the posture measurements and symptoms; review medication and volume status with individualized management and fall-risk advice. Recheck standing pressure. Persistent symptoms call for reassessment and consideration of specialist evaluation. New acute features would require a separate urgency decision.

nr-101.assessment: The witnessed convulsive episode, post-event confusion and lateral tongue injury support a first suspected epileptic seizure. Onset and cause remain unclassified. Initial ECG and metabolic evaluation are reassuring but not exhaustive. The later normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy.
nr-101.plan: Complete a first-seizure specialist assessment, using the cited NICE urgent referral pathway as the course example. Provide individual interim safety advice and a contact plan if another event occurs. Arrange further testing and any treatment according to the specialist assessment; do not select a permanent regimen or withdraw precautions solely because the routine EEG is normal.

interview.prompt: Ask about the fainting episodes and recovery
interview.finding: He had three abrupt syncopal episodes in two days without warning, followed by quick recovery and no postictal confusion, tongue injury, or head trauma.

interview.prompt: Ask about symptoms between episodes
interview.finding: Between events he feels fatigued, dizzy, and short of breath with minimal exertion. He has noticed a very slow pulse at home.

interview.prompt: Review cardiac history and medications
interview.finding: History includes prior anterior MI, hypertension, and diabetes. Medications include metoprolol 50 mg daily; there were no recent medication changes or illnesses.

exam.finding: He is alert but pale and fatigued, mildly hypotensive and bradycardic, with mildly delayed capillary refill.

exam.prompt: Examine the heart and neck veins
exam.finding: The rhythm is slow and regular with varying S1 intensity and occasional cannon A waves. There is no murmur or gallop.

exam.prompt: Perform a focused neurologic and pulmonary exam
exam.finding: The neurologic exam is nonfocal, lungs are clear, and there is no peripheral edema.

interview.prompt: Characterize the palpitations
interview.finding: The fast, regular pounding began abruptly 40 minutes ago at rest. Several similar episodes over the past year ended spontaneously within minutes.

interview.prompt: Ask about instability or cardiopulmonary symptoms
interview.finding: She has mild lightheadedness and throat fluttering but denies chest pain, syncope, or significant dyspnea.

interview.prompt: Ask about triggers and arrhythmia risks
interview.finding: She drinks two to three coffees daily and had extra caffeine today. She has no cardiac history, recent illness, thyroid symptoms, recreational stimulant or sympathomimetic drug use, or family history of sudden death.

exam.finding: She is alert, mildly anxious, normally mentating, and well perfused without respiratory distress.

exam.prompt: Auscultate the heart and check the pulse
exam.finding: There is a rapid, regular tachycardia with normal heart sounds, no murmur, and rapid regular peripheral pulses of good volume.

exam.prompt: Look for heart-failure or thyroid findings
exam.finding: Lungs are clear, there is no JVD or edema, and the neck has no thyromegaly.

interview.prompt: Ask about the injury and symptom timeline
interview.finding: He struck his head on tile 10 days ago. After only a brief initial headache, he developed three days of worsening headache, drowsiness, confusion, gait difficulty, and vomiting.

interview.prompt: Review bleeding risk and medications
interview.finding: He has atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin and believes his recent INR was a little high. He also drinks alcohol regularly.

interview.prompt: Ask about new focal or infectious symptoms
interview.finding: His wife reports new word-finding difficulty and right-hand clumsiness. He has had no fever, neck stiffness, or seizures.

exam.finding: He is drowsy but arousable and oriented to person and place, but not date.
There is right pronator drift, subtle right-hand clumsiness, mild word-finding hesitancy, and a wide-based unsteady gait.

exam.prompt: Look for trauma and raised-pressure clues
exam.finding: There is left parietal scalp tenderness without laceration. Pupils are equal and reactive, and no papilledema or neck rigidity is seen.

interview.prompt: Ask about the pain and skin progression
interview.finding: Perineal and scrotal pain, swelling, and discoloration worsened rapidly over 24 hours, with pain far out of proportion and a crackling sensation.

interview.prompt: Ask about infection source and risk factors
interview.finding: He has poorly controlled diabetes, obesity, tobacco use, and a perianal abscess drained two weeks ago. He now reports foul-smelling discharge.

interview.prompt: Ask about systemic symptoms
interview.finding: He has fever, chills, malaise, nausea, poor intake, and orthostatic lightheadedness.

exam.finding: Dusky erythematous-to-violaceous skin, tense edema, areas of necrosis, and foul serosanguinous discharge are present.

exam.prompt: Palpate for extent, tenderness, and crepitus
exam.finding: Tenderness extends beyond the erythema with palpable crepitus, patchy anesthesia, and pain out of proportion extending toward the lower abdominal wall.
He is toxic, diaphoretic, tachycardic, and hypotensive with delayed capillary refill.

interview.prompt: Ask about pregnancy possibility and bleeding
interview.finding: Her last menstrual period was about seven weeks ago. She has had two days of light vaginal spotting and uses condoms inconsistently.

interview.prompt: Characterize the pain and collapse
interview.finding: Sudden severe left lower-quadrant pain became diffuse, followed by near-syncope, increasing weakness, feeling cold, and new right shoulder discomfort.

interview.prompt: Ask about ectopic-pregnancy risks
interview.finding: She has a prior medically managed ectopic pregnancy and a history of chlamydial pelvic inflammatory disease.

exam.finding: She is pale, diaphoretic, cool, clammy, and slow to respond, with delayed capillary refill.
The abdomen is diffusely tender, worst in the left lower quadrant, with guarding, rebound, and mild distension.
There is scant dark blood at the cervical os, marked cervical-motion tenderness, and severe left adnexal tenderness with fullness.

interview.prompt: Characterize the chest discomfort
interview.finding: He describes a tight substernal band radiating to the left shoulder, lasting three to five minutes and resolving completely with rest.

interview.prompt: Ask about pattern and unstable features
interview.finding: Symptoms occur reliably after two uphill blocks or two flights of stairs and have not changed for three months. There is no rest or nocturnal pain.

interview.prompt: Review vascular risks and medications
interview.finding: He has hypertension, hyperlipidemia, a 30 pack-year smoking history, and paternal MI at 58. He often misses atorvastatin doses.

exam.prompt: Examine the heart, lungs, and neck veins
exam.finding: Heart sounds and rhythm are normal without murmur, rub, or gallop; lungs are clear and JVP is not elevated.

exam.prompt: Assess pulses, bruits, and volume status
exam.finding: Pulses are symmetric, no carotid or femoral bruits are heard, and there is no edema or abdominal pulsatile mass.

exam.prompt: Try to reproduce the pain mechanically
exam.finding: The chest wall is nontender, and pain is not reproduced by palpation, arm movement, or deep inspiration.

interview.prompt: Ask about onset and concerning symptoms
interview.finding: Palpitations began abruptly six hours ago with mild exertional breathlessness and fatigue. There is no chest pain, syncope, fever, or cough.

interview.prompt: Ask about possible triggers
interview.finding: He drank five or six alcoholic drinks at a wedding last night, far more than usual, and denies stimulant or decongestant use.

interview.prompt: Review stroke-risk history
interview.finding: He is 68 with hypertension and diabetes, but no prior stroke, heart failure, or vascular disease.

exam.prompt: Assess the cardiac rhythm and pulse
exam.finding: There is an irregularly irregular tachycardia with variable S1 and a radial pulse deficit.

exam.prompt: Look for poor perfusion or heart failure
exam.finding: He is alert, warm, and well perfused. Lungs are clear, JVP is normal, and there is no edema.
The thyroid is normal in size without nodules, and there is no tremor.

interview.prompt: Clarify the collapse and recovery
interview.finding: He collapsed without warning while sprinting, was unresponsive for about 20 seconds, and awoke immediately oriented without tongue injury, incontinence, or confusion.

interview.prompt: Ask about prior exertional symptoms
interview.finding: He admits to two prior lightheaded spells during sprints and occasional exertional chest tightness.

interview.prompt: Ask about family cardiac history
interview.finding: A paternal uncle died suddenly at 38 while swimming, and his father was once told he had thick heart walls.

exam.finding: A harsh systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border and apex grows louder with Valsalva and standing, and softens with squatting and handgrip.

exam.prompt: Assess the precordium and carotid pulse
exam.finding: The PMI is forceful but nondisplaced, an S4 is present, and the carotid upstroke is brisk and bifid without carotid radiation.

exam.prompt: Perform a neurologic and volume-status exam
exam.finding: Neurologic findings are normal; JVP is normal, lungs are clear, and there is no edema.

interview.prompt: Ask about infectious and constitutional symptoms
interview.finding: He has had 10 days of fever, drenching night sweats, fatigue, anorexia, and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss.

interview.prompt: Ask about injection practices and exposure risks
interview.finding: He injects heroin several times daily, reuses needles, has unstable housing, and has never been tested for HIV.

interview.prompt: Ask about pulmonary or embolic symptoms
interview.finding: For three days he has had pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, and a productive cough occasionally streaked with blood.

exam.prompt: Examine the heart and neck veins
exam.finding: A soft holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border augments with inspiration; JVP is mildly elevated.

exam.prompt: Examine the lungs and respiratory status
exam.finding: He is in mild respiratory distress with scattered bilateral crackles.

exam.prompt: Look for injection sites and endocarditis stigmata
exam.finding: Fresh and healed track marks are present. No splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, or conjunctival lesions are identified.

interview.prompt: Characterize the acute chest pain
interview.finding: Severe substernal pressure radiating to the left arm began suddenly at rest one hour ago with diaphoresis and nausea.

interview.prompt: Ask about pregnancy and postpartum timing
interview.finding: She delivered her first child by uncomplicated vaginal delivery three weeks ago and is currently breastfeeding.

interview.prompt: Review coronary and vascular risks
interview.finding: She has no diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, smoking, cocaine use, or premature family coronary disease. Prior renal imaging noted mild fibromuscular features.

exam.finding: She is anxious and diaphoretic with ongoing chest pain but remains hemodynamically stable and well perfused.
Heart sounds and rhythm are normal without murmur, gallop, or rub; lungs are clear and there are no signs of heart failure.

exam.prompt: Look for vascular asymmetry or thromboembolism
exam.finding: Pulses are symmetric, no bruits are heard, and there is no edema or calf tenderness.

interview.prompt: Ask about timing and positional triggers
interview.finding: Spinning begins seconds after rolling right, looking up, or bending forward, lasts 20 to 40 seconds, and resolves completely between spells.

interview.prompt: Ask about auditory symptoms
interview.finding: She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, or ear fullness.

interview.prompt: Screen for central neurologic symptoms
interview.finding: She denies headache, diplopia, dysarthria, numbness, weakness, or gait difficulty between episodes.

exam.prompt: Inspect for spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus
exam.finding: No spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus is present while she sits comfortably between spells.
Coordination, regular and tandem gait, and Romberg testing are normal.
Hearing is grossly symmetric and otoscopy shows normal mobile tympanic membranes without effusion.

interview.prompt: Obtain a witness description of the event
interview.finding: He cried out, became rigid, and had generalized shaking for 60 to 90 seconds with frothing and urinary incontinence, followed by about 20 minutes of confusion.

interview.prompt: Ask about potential provoking factors
interview.finding: He has slept only three to four hours nightly but denies drugs, heavy alcohol use or withdrawal, trauma, fever, or headache.

interview.prompt: Ask about prior and family seizure history
interview.finding: He has never had a seizure, takes no medications, and has no family history of epilepsy or sudden death.

exam.finding: He is fully alert and back to baseline. A fresh laceration is present on the left lateral tongue.
Cranial nerves, strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination, gait, and Romberg testing are normal.

exam.prompt: Look for infection or systemic illness
exam.finding: There is no neck stiffness, photophobia, rash, or cardiopulmonary abnormality.

interview.prompt: Clarify duration and positional behavior
interview.finding: Severe vertigo has been continuous for 18 hours and persists at rest, although any head movement worsens it. He has vomited four times.

interview.prompt: Ask about hearing and ear symptoms
interview.finding: He denies hearing change, tinnitus, or ear fullness.

interview.prompt: Screen for central symptoms and vascular risks
interview.finding: He denies headache, neck pain, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, sensory loss, or weakness. He has hypertension and a 20 pack-year smoking history.

exam.finding: Spontaneous horizontal left-beating nystagmus intensifies on left gaze, lessens on right gaze, and dampens with visual fixation.

exam.prompt: Test cranial nerves and limb coordination
exam.finding: Hearing, speech, facial function, strength, and finger-to-nose testing are normal, without limb ataxia.
He can stand unassisted but veers to the right while walking.

interview.prompt: Clarify the injury and lucid interval
interview.finding: He was struck over the left temple, lost consciousness for about one minute, then woke and conversed normally before later deterioration.

interview.prompt: Ask about symptom progression
interview.finding: Over 30 minutes he developed severe worsening left-sided headache, two episodes of vomiting, confusion, and increasing sleepiness.

interview.prompt: Review medications and bleeding risks
interview.finding: He takes no medications or anticoagulants, has no known bleeding disorder, and drank two beers earlier.

exam.finding: GCS is 11. The left pupil is 5 mm and sluggish; the right is 3 mm and brisk.
There is right pronator drift, right-sided 4-/5 weakness, symmetric reflexes, and an extensor right plantar response.
A boggy hematoma overlies the left temporal scalp. No battle sign or raccoon eyes are present yet.

interview.prompt: Ask about onset and recent neck events
interview.finding: Right neck and facial pain began the day after cervical spinal manipulation; ptosis and a smaller right pupil developed over the next two days.

interview.prompt: Ask about visual and Horner-type symptoms
interview.finding: He noticed partial right eyelid droop and miosis but denies diplopia or vision loss.

interview.prompt: Screen for transient neurologic symptoms and vascular risks
interview.finding: He had brief left-hand tingling that resolved, without current weakness or dysarthria. He has no major medical or smoking history.

exam.prompt: Examine pupils, eyelids, and eye movements
exam.finding: There is partial right ptosis and reactive right miosis with preserved facial sweating. Eye movements, acuity, and visual fields are normal.
Apart from the right partial ptosis and reactive miosis, speech, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, coordination, and gait are normal.

exam.prompt: Examine the neck and carotid region
exam.finding: The right anterolateral neck is tender, but no carotid bruit is heard and the cardiac rhythm is regular.

interview.prompt: Ask the witness about onset and recovery
interview.finding: Prolonged standing at a blood draw; warmth and sweating before collapse, pallor, three brief jerks, and immediate orientation on awakening.

interview.prompt: Ask about exertion, cardiac symptoms and family history
interview.finding: No exertional trigger, palpitation, chest pain, known cardiac disease or early familial sudden death.

interview.prompt: Ask about injury and persistent symptoms
interview.finding: She was lowered to the floor, has no head or tongue injury, and has fully recovered.

exam.finding: Fully oriented with no focal deficit or injury.
Regular pulse and no audible murmur; current vital signs are stable.

exam.prompt: Assess symptoms with a safe change in posture
exam.finding: Supported standing does not reproduce symptoms in this assessment.

interview.prompt: Ask about posture, prodrome and recovery
interview.finding: Symptoms occur after getting up and improve lying down. The brief collapse was followed by prompt recovery.

interview.prompt: Review medications, intake and bleeding symptoms
interview.finding: A thiazide was recently introduced; intake fell during hot weather. He reports no bleeding. These are possible contributors.

interview.prompt: Ask about cardiac red flags
interview.finding: No exertional event, chest pain, palpitation or early family history of sudden death is reported.

exam.prompt: Assess whether posture measurements can be performed safely
exam.finding: He is stable lying down and can stand with staff support; he will be assisted if symptoms recur.
Mildly dry mucous membranes; regular pulse, no significant murmur or pulmonary congestion.

exam.prompt: Check for injury or focal neurologic findings
exam.finding: No injury or focal deficit is identified.

interview.prompt: Ask the witness about movements, duration and recovery
interview.finding: Bilateral stiffening and jerking lasted about 90 seconds, followed by about 15 minutes of confusion. Earliest onset was not clearly observed.

interview.prompt: Ask about triggers and possible provoking factors
interview.finding: No posture-related prodrome, fever, trauma or alcohol withdrawal is reported; she describes no previous episode.

interview.prompt: Ask about current recovery and remaining symptoms
interview.finding: She has returned to baseline and reports no persistent headache or focal symptom.

exam.prompt: Assess current mental status and neurologic findings
exam.finding: Fully oriented, nonfocal examination and no meningism.
Small lateral tongue injury; no significant head injury is identified.
Regular pulse, no audible murmur and stable current vital signs.

em-016.objective: Prioritize stability and distinguish a regular narrow-complex rhythm.
em-016.alternativesAndLimits: Modified Valsalva is the preferred teaching maneuver here. Drug selection and cardioversion depend on the rhythm, contraindications, and stability.

learningLinks.title: Measure before naming an ECG pattern

em-018.objective: Recognize traumatic intracranial bleeding and coordinate reversal with urgent surgery.
em-018.alternativesAndLimits: Do not wait for worsening when the initial size, shift, and deficits already justify operative evaluation.

em-015.objective: Identify complete AV dissociation and respond to unstable bradycardia.
em-015.alternativesAndLimits: Medication support can accompany pacing preparation. Evaluate reversible causes; the exercise does not assess actual pacing competence.

Measure before naming an ECG pattern

em-020.objective: Recognize a necrotizing infection and coordinate resuscitation, antibiotics, and source control.
em-020.alternativesAndLimits: The shown imaging is available information, not a prerequisite for surgery. Antibiotic and fluid choices require individualized clinical assessment.

sources.title: IDSA skin and soft-tissue infection guideline

em-033.objective: Connect pregnancy, shock, and abdominal findings to urgent hemorrhage control.
em-033.alternativesAndLimits: An hCG threshold alone cannot locate a pregnancy. Operative approach and resuscitation depend on instability and available expertise.

learningLinks.title: Oxygen saturation is not oxygen content

cd-001.objective: Distinguish a stable symptom pattern and separate ischemia evidence from coronary anatomy.
cd-001.alternativesAndLimits: Exercise ECG is one reasonable pathway. Imaging-based assessment and alternative antianginal medicines may also be appropriate.

cd-006.objective: Interpret AF, choose context-appropriate rate control, and assess stroke prevention.
cd-006.alternativesAndLimits: The fictional case explicitly supplies preserved LVEF. Treatment changes with ventricular dysfunction, pre-excitation, instability, and valve disease.

cd-055.objective: Recognize dynamic obstruction and identify the need for specialist risk assessment.
cd-055.alternativesAndLimits: The immediate exercise pause follows recent syncope. Later sports participation and ICD decisions require individualized shared assessment.

cd-061.objective: Connect systemic infection and pulmonary embolic findings to a cardiac source.
cd-061.alternativesAndLimits: Cultures, empiric treatment, and echocardiography proceed promptly. The complete antibiotic regimen and duration depend on clinical and microbiologic findings.

cd-019.objective: Revise a management plan when initially stable coronary dissection deteriorates.
cd-019.alternativesAndLimits: The final note must reflect the later ischemia and hypotension, rather than simply repeating the initial conservative plan.

learningLinks.title: ST changes and troponin answer different questions

nr-011.objective: Use timing and positional findings to identify a treatable vestibular pattern.
nr-011.alternativesAndLimits: Check maneuver suitability and reassess persistent or atypical symptoms; recurrence alone is not a reason for indefinite suppressants.

nr-025.objective: Classify a first seizure and discuss treatment using individual recurrence risk.
nr-025.alternativesAndLimits: Both medication and deferral may be reasonable after counseling. Written responses are not graded against one compulsory treatment choice.

nr-012.objective: Interpret a vestibular examination within its training and syndrome limits.
nr-012.alternativesAndLimits: HINTS is not a novice self-test. Equivocal, unreliable, or evolving findings require further urgent assessment.

nr-016.objective: Connect trauma, focal deterioration, and CT findings to urgent decompression.
nr-016.alternativesAndLimits: Temporizing measures do not replace surgery. The CT supplies thickness and shift; hematoma volume was not provided.

nr-008.objective: Connect a painful partial Horner syndrome to arterial imaging and stroke prevention.
nr-008.alternativesAndLimits: Select antithrombotic treatment with the stroke team rather than treating available options as universally equivalent.

em-101.objective: Use event sequence to distinguish a likely faint from seizure and recognize a cardiac reason to reconsider.
em-101.alternativesAndLimits: Targeted testing remains appropriate when history or examination suggests another cause. The contrast question is not a newly discovered fact about this patient. Local follow-up pathways vary.
